title: The Customer Meeting
subtitle: How one sales call becomes memory, intelligence, and action
description: Follow a single sales call from the moment it happens to the moment the Brain generates a risk alert and delivers context to the account manager's Gmail — automatically.

steps.title: The Meeting Happens
steps.narrative: A sales call with Acme Corp. Maria (Account Manager), Sarah (AE), and the client's VP of Engineering are on the call. Three things happen: a delayed proposal is discussed, a new technical requirement is raised, and Maria verbally commits to delivering an updated proposal by end of Q3.
steps.technical_detail: No Brain involvement yet. This is organizational reality: actors communicating, a commitment being made, a goal being discussed. The Capture layer is observing passively — it has not yet interpreted anything.
steps.visual_hint: Three people on a call. A calendar. A transcript appearing.

steps.title: The Brain Observes
steps.narrative: The Brain ingests the meeting: the calendar event, the transcript from the recording, and the CRM notes Sarah logged afterward. Raw signals. No understanding yet — just capture.
steps.technical_detail: Capture layer ingests: calendar metadata (participants, time, duration), transcript (full text), CRM notes (structured by Sarah). All signals timestamped and source-tagged. No interpretation at this stage — outputs are raw activity, raw events, raw communications.

steps.title: Breaking It Into Building Blocks
steps.narrative: The Understanding layer reads the meeting and identifies the building blocks present. It finds: four Actors (Maria, Sarah, the VP, Acme Corp), the Communication (the meeting itself), one Commitment (the Q3 proposal promise), a Goal (Q3 renewal), and the Relationship (Maria manages Sarah; Acme is a customer).
steps.technical_detail: Understanding layer applies the ten Atomic Primitives: Actor, Communication, Commitment, Action, Resource, Rule, Goal, State, Time, Relationship. Every organizational event decomposes into these. Decision, Meeting, Project are composites — reconstructed from these primitives, never stored as their own primitive.
steps.visual_hint: The meeting breaking into labelled blocks.

steps.title: Creating the Filing Cards
steps.narrative: The Brain creates structured representations — Knowledge Objects — for each entity identified. A Person Object for Maria. A Person Object for the VP. A Meeting Object for the call. A Commitment Object for the Q3 promise. A Customer Object for Acme Corp. These are the Brain's standardized filing format.
steps.technical_detail: Knowledge Objects are canonical representations — human-readable, AI-readable, traceable, versionable, portable. They are NOT memory. They are the representation layer from which memory is formed. Primitive Knowledge Objects (Actor, Communication, Commitment, etc.) map directly to Atomic Primitives. Composite Knowledge Objects (Meeting, Person, Customer) are built by combining Primitive Knowledge Objects, per the Ontology.

steps.title: Filing Into the Right Stores
steps.narrative: The Knowledge Objects are routed to the right memory stores. Who attended → Factual Memory. Why the discussion happened and what alternatives were considered → Interaction Memory. The Q3 commitment Maria made → Commitment Memory, in state Promised. What actions were taken so far → Action Memory receives nothing yet — nothing has been executed.
steps.technical_detail: Memory formation routing: Factual Memory receives stable organizational reality (people, accounts, goals). Interaction Memory receives the discussion and reasoning. Commitment Memory receives the Commitment Object with lifecycle state Promised. Action Memory receives nothing — no execution has occurred yet. Every record carries provenance: source (transcript), asserted by (Understanding layer), confidence (High), timestamp. One meeting can create records in multiple memory types simultaneously, all sharing a common source reference.

steps.title: The Brain Connects the Dots
steps.narrative: The Intelligence layer reads across all five memory stores. It detects: the Q3 commitment is now 30 days old with no progress recorded. Acme Corp's last engagement in Interaction Memory was 3 weeks ago. The Q3 revenue goal in Factual Memory is $2.4M. Two intelligence objects are generated: an Operational Risk ('Q3 renewal at risk') and a Recommendation ('Schedule executive check-in with Acme this week').
steps.technical_detail: Intelligence layer queries: Commitment Memory (open commitments with no linked Action), Interaction Memory (last engagement timestamp), Factual Memory (account goal, revenue target). Pattern: commitment + silence + goal = risk. Operational Risk lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Tracked → Resolved. Recommendation lifecycle: Draft → Presented → Accepted/Rejected/Modified. Both carry Owner (Maria Lopez), Confidence (High), and a Review Trigger (Acme meeting scheduled).
steps.visual_hint: Connections forming between memory stores. Two alert cards appearing.

steps.title: Delivered at the Right Moment
steps.narrative: Maria opens Gmail to write to the Acme VP. Inside her compose window — without switching apps, without searching — the Brain surfaces: the Q3 risk flag, the unfulfilled commitment status, Sarah's last engagement date, and a suggested action. Maria didn't ask for any of this. The Brain delivered it at exactly the moment she needed it.
steps.technical_detail: Exposure layer — Ambient Delivery mode. Brain integrates with Gmail via browser extension. Trigger: compose window opens to a known contact (Acme VP). Brain queries all memory related to Acme Corp + sender (Maria) + recipient and assembles a context package. Design rule: the Brain never interrupts and remains silent when no useful memory exists. Every suggestion is contextual, dismissible, explainable, and traceable.

steps.title: Learning From What Happened
steps.narrative: Maria accepts the recommendation. She schedules the Acme check-in. The Brain records the outcome. If this same pattern — commitment + silence + risk + recommendation accepted — occurs across other accounts independently, the Brain proposes a new heuristic: 'Commitments with no progress after 30 days need a prompt.' That learning is proposed to Memory and approved.
steps.technical_detail: Evolution layer: Recommendation outcome logged (Accepted) — a terminal state, so confidence is frozen and stops decaying. This single acceptance is not yet a learning pattern (Single Feedback ≠ Learning). A second, independently-occurring instance of the same pattern — different commitment, different account — would qualify as Repeated Validated Feedback. Only then is a Learning Memory candidate proposed, and it still passes through Memory Model's standard Write Governance (AI proposes, human or policy-owner approves) before it becomes memory. Intelligence never writes directly to memory.

title: The Missed Commitment
subtitle: A Q3 promise nobody followed up on — and how the Brain catches it anyway
description: Follow a single promise from the moment it's made through silence, breach, escalation, and resolution — and see exactly what the Brain's audit trail preserves along the way.

steps.title: The Promise Is Made
steps.narrative: In a Q2 business review, Sarah tells the Acme Corp team: 'I'll have the updated pricing proposal to you by end of Q3.' It's a single sentence in a longer conversation — easy to miss, easy to forget.
steps.technical_detail: Understanding extracts a Commitment primitive from this Communication: Actor = Sarah, obligated to = Acme Corp, deliverable = updated pricing proposal, due = end of Q3 (Sep 30). Commitment Memory creates a record in state Promised. No Action has occurred yet.

steps.title: Time Passes. Nothing Happens.
steps.narrative: Weeks go by. No draft is shared. No follow-up email is sent. No one mentions it again — not Sarah, not her manager Maria, not anyone at Acme. From the outside, it looks like nothing is wrong, because nothing is happening at all.
steps.technical_detail: Capture continues observing — there's simply no new signal to capture. Commitment Memory's record stays in state Promised. The Time primitive on the record keeps accumulating: days since last activity, days until due date.

steps.title: The Brain Notices The Silence
steps.narrative: Sep 30 passes. No Action Memory record exists linking back to this Commitment — no proposal was ever delivered. The Brain doesn't wait for someone to notice; it checks automatically.
steps.technical_detail: Intelligence evaluates open Commitments against their due dates as part of routine Commitment Evaluation. With the due date passed and no fulfilling Action recorded, the Commitment's state transitions from Promised to Breached — this is a Memory Layer state change, not yet an Intelligence output by itself.

steps.title: Operational Risk Generated
steps.narrative: The Brain cross-references the breach against Factual Memory: Acme Corp is linked to a $200k Q3 revenue goal. A breached commitment tied to a real revenue target isn't just a missed task — it's a risk to something the business actually cares about.
steps.technical_detail: Risk Intelligence generates an Operational Risk: sources = the Breached Commitment + the linked Goal, confidence = High (direct evidence, no ambiguity), severity = High. Per the Confidence Model's asymmetric handling rule, this is surfaced immediately — Operational Risk is never withheld for being 'just one missed task.'

steps.title: A Recommendation Is Generated
steps.narrative: Alongside the risk, the Brain generates a concrete next step: someone should reach out to Acme now, acknowledge the delay, and give a real timeline — before Acme notices the silence themselves.
steps.technical_detail: Recommendation Intelligence produces: 'Escalate to Maria (Sarah's manager) and contact Acme directly. Commitment breached 3 days ago, no recorded progress. Owner: Maria Lopez. Confidence: High.' The Recommendation's owner is deliberately the manager, not just Sarah — escalation routing follows the Authority Model.

steps.title: Maria Finds Out — Without Searching
steps.narrative: Maria didn't check a dashboard. She opens her email Monday morning and the Brain has already surfaced the risk and recommendation in her Personal Reality view, with full context: what was promised, to whom, how long it's been silent, and what to do next.
steps.technical_detail: Exposure layer delivers via Ambient Delivery (Personal Reality surface, per Product Architecture's Mission Control mapping for Operational Risk). The design rule holds even here: the Brain doesn't interrupt with a popup — it's there, contextual and dismissible, when Maria naturally checks her morning view.

steps.title: Resolved — But Never Erased
steps.narrative: Maria reaches out to Sarah and to Acme directly. The proposal goes out a week late, with an apology. The commitment is eventually marked Fulfilled — but the breach itself is never deleted from the record. If this same pattern — a commitment with no check-in until it breaches — happens independently across a few other accounts, it becomes a real lesson.
steps.technical_detail: The original Breached state is preserved permanently in the audit trail even after a later Action fulfills the commitment late — Memory Model's Conflict Resolution never silently overwrites history. If the same pattern (silence → breach → late recovery) recurs across 2+ independent accounts, Evolution proposes a Learning Memory candidate: 'Commitments with no progress after 30 days should trigger an automatic check-in prompt' — which itself must pass through Memory's Write Governance before being approved.

title: The New Team Member
subtitle: Why do we use this architecture? — answered without interrupting anyone's day
description: A new engineer asks the question every new hire eventually asks. Follow how Interaction Memory answers it with the actual original reasoning, not a guess from whoever's nearby.

steps.title: The Question Every New Hire Asks
steps.narrative: James joins the engineering team in his second week. Looking through the codebase, he asks in Slack: 'why do we use microservices here instead of a monolith? Seems like a lot of overhead for our team size.' Nobody currently active on the team was actually in the room when that decision was made 14 months ago.
steps.technical_detail: This is organizational reality, not yet a Brain interaction — a Communication (James's question) with an implicit Knowledge Gap behind it: the reasoning behind a foundational decision isn't living in anyone currently on the team's head.

steps.title: James Asks The Brain Instead Of Interrupting Someone
steps.narrative: Instead of pinging the VP of Engineering and waiting for a free moment in her day, James asks Claude directly: 'why did we choose microservices over a monolith?' Claude doesn't know — but it knows where to ask.
steps.technical_detail: Claude queries the Brain via MCP (brain_search / brain_get_context) rather than answering from general knowledge. This is Agent Access: the Brain serving as an MCP provider so any AI tool can retrieve governed, sourced organizational memory instead of guessing.

steps.title: The Brain Retrieves The Original Reasoning
steps.narrative: The Brain doesn't have a 'decision' record to hand back — because Decisions aren't stored directly. Instead, it pulls the original architecture review meeting from Interaction Memory: who was there, what alternatives were discussed, and who objected.
steps.technical_detail: Interaction Memory record retrieved: meeting from 14 months ago. Contains the full discussion — not just the outcome. This is exactly Interaction Memory's purpose: preserving reasoning so it doesn't die with the people who made it.

steps.title: Reconstructing The Decision
steps.narrative: The Brain doesn't just dump the transcript — it reconstructs the actual Decision from its component parts: the discussion, the goal it served, the rule that governed it, and the commitment it created.
steps.technical_detail: Decision = Communication (the architecture review discussion) + Goal ('scale to 10x traffic without a full rewrite') + Rule (the engineering RFC approval policy) + Commitment (adopt microservices, owned by the then-CTO, due by Q2 of last year). This is Ontology's Operational Constructs layer at work — Decision is never stored as its own object, only ever reconstructed.

steps.title: The Answer, With Sources Attached
steps.narrative: Claude answers James with the real reasoning: the team considered a monolith with horizontal scaling first, the then-CTO actually preferred it initially, but the deciding factor was team topology — five small teams needed independent deploy cycles. Every part of that answer links back to the original meeting record.
steps.technical_detail: Exposure delivers via Agent Access context injection. Every claim in the answer is traceable: this is the Evidence behind the Claim — the meeting record, its date, and its attendees — not a confident-sounding guess. James can click through to the original Interaction Memory record himself if he wants the full transcript.

steps.title: The Question Itself Becomes A Signal
steps.narrative: James isn't the first new hire to ask this exact question — three other engineers asked something similar in their first month over the past year. That repetition is itself worth noticing.
steps.technical_detail: If the same Knowledge Gap pattern (new hires repeatedly missing this specific context) recurs across multiple independent onboarding cohorts, Evolution can propose it as a candidate process improvement — e.g., surfacing this exact Interaction Memory record automatically during onboarding — through the same Learning Memory write path as any other validated pattern.

title: The Policy That Wasn't Followed
subtitle: A team skips an approval step under deadline pressure — and it's not the first time
description: Follow one skipped approval from the moment it happens through detection, escalation, a formal Challenge, and a governed Exception — and see how a single incident becomes the evidence for fixing the real, structural problem.

steps.title: The Approval Gets Skipped
steps.narrative: Under deadline pressure, the sales team executes a $120k contract with Acme Corp without the required CFO sign-off. The plan is to get the approval afterward — 'just this once,' to keep the deal on schedule.
steps.technical_detail: This is organizational reality, not yet a Brain interaction. The Rule in Factual Memory ('contracts above $100k require CFO signature') exists and is unaffected. An Action occurs (contract executed) with no corresponding Approval record.

steps.title: Captured Like Any Other Action
steps.narrative: Nothing dramatic happens at the moment it's signed. The contract execution is captured and understood like any other Action — it's only when the Brain checks it against policy that anything looks different.
steps.technical_detail: Action Memory records the contract execution: Actor, Resource (the contract), timestamp, outcome. No flag is raised yet — Action Memory just preserves what happened, observed reality, without judgment.

steps.title: Policy Violation Detected
steps.narrative: The Brain compares the executed contract against the Rule that governs it and finds no Approval record where one is required. This is one specific, identifiable breach — not a hunch, not a future risk. It happened.
steps.technical_detail: Policy Violation generated: 'Contract C-2024-089 ($120k) executed without CFO signature. Policy mandates CFO approval above $100k.' Owner: CFO Office. Lifecycle: Detected → Validated (confirmed by reviewing approval records).

steps.title: Wait — This Has Happened Before
steps.narrative: Before escalating, the Brain checks Action Memory for similar cases. This is the third approval skip in two months, across two different teams. A single skip might be a fluke. Three independent ones are a pattern.
steps.technical_detail: Drift Intelligence re-evaluates: a Drift Candidate (this one instance) joins two prior independent instances to form a Drift Pattern, and with confidence now ≥ Medium per the Confidence Model, escalates to a confirmed Drift Signal: 'CFO approval step bypassed in 3 of 14 contracts over 90 days, across 2 teams. Severity: Medium.'

steps.title: Escalated, Then Challenged
steps.narrative: The Policy Violation escalates to the CFO's office. The Sales Lead responsible raises a formal Challenge: the deal was time-sensitive and low-risk, and she argues it should be accepted after the fact rather than treated as a violation requiring correction.
steps.technical_detail: Challenge Lifecycle: Raised (by the Sales Lead, who has standing) → Reviewed (CFO's office examines the deal terms and risk profile) → moving toward Resolved. This is a human-initiated dispute, distinct from Memory Model's automatic Conflict Resolution.

steps.title: A Governed Exception, Not A Quiet Pass
steps.narrative: The CFO reviews the evidence and agrees the deal itself was low-risk — but instead of just letting it slide, a formal Exception is proposed, reviewed, and approved: time-bound, with conditions, fully on the record.
steps.technical_detail: Exception Lifecycle: Proposed → Reviewed → Approved → Active. This formally closes the Policy Violation via acceptance rather than correction — the deviation is visible and accountable, not quietly ignored. It will Expire automatically, restoring full enforcement.

steps.title: Fixing The Real Problem, Not Just This Case
steps.narrative: One contract is resolved. But the Drift Signal — three skips across two teams — is still open, and it's pointing at something structural: maybe the approval process itself is too slow for time-sensitive deals.
steps.technical_detail: Because this is a confirmed Drift Signal (not just one Policy Violation), Evolution proposes a process improvement candidate: 'Add an expedited approval path for time-sensitive contracts under $150k.' Like any Learning Memory candidate, it must pass through Memory's Write Governance — proposed by Intelligence, approved by a human with the right authority — before it changes how the organization actually operates.

title: The AI Agent Preparing A Proposal
subtitle: Claude asks the Brain instead of guessing — and the proposal shows it
description: Follow what happens when an account manager asks an AI assistant to draft a renewal proposal — and see exactly how governed, sourced memory turns a generic first draft into a genuinely informed one.

steps.title: The Ask
steps.narrative: Maria, the account manager for Acme Corp, opens Claude and types: 'Prepare a renewal proposal for Acme Corp.' Without any other context, that's a request an AI can only answer generically — or guess.
steps.technical_detail: This is organizational reality plus an AI tool — no Brain involvement yet. The request itself is a Communication, directed at an AI Actor rather than a human one.

steps.title: Claude Asks The Brain Instead Of Guessing
steps.narrative: Rather than producing a generic proposal template, Claude recognizes it needs real account context and queries the Company Brain directly — the same way a well-prepared colleague would pull up the account file before writing anything.
steps.technical_detail: Claude calls the Brain's MCP surface — brain_get_context and brain_get_commitments for Acme Corp — rather than relying on general knowledge. This is Agent Access: the Brain acting as an MCP provider, governed identically for AI as for human access.

steps.title: Real Context Gets Assembled
steps.narrative: The Brain doesn't hand back a document — it assembles a contextual package: who Acme Corp is and what the contract is worth, what's currently promised and outstanding, and what was discussed and decided in past negotiations.
steps.technical_detail: Context Assembly pulls from Factual Memory (account details, contract value, goal linkage), Commitment Memory (an overdue pricing proposal commitment), and Interaction Memory (reasoning from the last renewal negotiation) into one bounded Context Package.

steps.title: Risk Comes Attached, Not Hidden
steps.narrative: The context isn't just facts — it includes the Operational Risk already on file: Acme hasn't been meaningfully engaged in 60 days, and a commitment from the last review is still unresolved. Claude's draft can now address this directly instead of ignoring it.
steps.technical_detail: The Operational Risk object (confidence: High, owner: Maria) is included in the context package alongside its sources — not summarized away. This is exactly Intelligence Architecture's explainability principle: every conclusion carries its evidence.

steps.title: The Draft Is Built On Governed Memory
steps.narrative: Claude writes the proposal referencing the real contract history, acknowledges the engagement gap directly, and proposes next steps consistent with what was actually discussed before — not a generic template with the company name swapped in.
steps.technical_detail: Every claim in the draft is traceable back to a source Maria can inspect — this is the Claim/Evidence relationship at work even inside an AI-generated artifact. Knowledge Exchange principles apply here too: governance and provenance travel with the memory, even when consumed by an external AI tool.

steps.title: Maria Reviews, Sends, And The Loop Closes
steps.narrative: Maria reads a draft that's actually informed — not one she has to fact-check from scratch. She makes one small edit and sends it. The Brain logs what happened, closing the loop back into memory.
steps.technical_detail: The sent proposal is recorded as an Action, linked back to the original overdue Commitment. If agent-assisted drafts like this one are accepted with minimal edits across multiple independent cases, that becomes a feedback signal Evolution can eventually act on — but never from a single instance.
